head:
Children and teenagers · Causes of the decline

Screens, sleep, school sport: where has movement gone

Young people run less well than at the start of the 1980s, and everyone has an explanation. Screens come first, even though they are the cause with the thinnest numbers. This article takes the proposed causes one by one and applies the same tests to each. It says what is solid, what is weak and what no study read can tell us.

The problem

When people talk about young people moving less, everyone has an explanation: screens, shrinking sleep, school sport that supposedly is not what it was, the car because the street is not safe, cities built for cars. Every sentence sounds right, and that is the problem: an explanation that sounds right can be wrong, or true but tiny.

Causes also get mixed together. A child who sleeps little may watch more screens and move less because he or she is tired. When two things go together, we do not know which one drives the other, or whether a third pulls both: that is the difference between association and cause, the thread of this article.

Still, each cause can be put to four questions. Does the link with movement exist in young people, and how big is it? Is there anything more than a snapshot of one moment (a follow-up over time, a trial) to say that the cause comes before the effect? Do the timing and the size of the cause match those of the decline? And if we act on it, does it bring improvement?

The question

Among the causes put forward to explain why young people move and run less well than before (screens, sleep, school sport, journeys, neighbourhood, safety), which are backed by numbers, with what level of evidence, and which can we act on without waiting for a verdict?

Six steps, from the most general to the most precise: the finding to be explained, screens, sleep, school sport, journeys and neighbourhood, then the objections.

What is at stake

First, there is long-term health. A review of 21 studies, which followed 6,197 people for 20.8 years on average, finds that endurance in childhood or adolescence partly carries over into adulthood: a correlation of 0.38, judged moderate, with large differences between studies.27 This does not say that everything is decided before 18, but that a low starting level is a probable handicap: the authors recommend building fitness early, because low fitness in adulthood is linked to chronic disease and mortality.27

Then there is the moment when it is decided. In France, according to the Esteban survey, 70% of boys and 56% of girls aged 6 to 10 reach the recommended 60 minutes of activity a day, then 34% and 20% at 11-14, and 40% and 16% at 15-17.7 Movement collapses on entry to lower secondary school, and adolescent girls are the furthest from the target.

Finally, there is a decision at stake. Limiting screens costs conflict at home, adding sport costs budget, making journeys safer costs building work. Choosing for the wrong reasons means aiming at the most visible cause rather than the most effective one, and making families carry a fault that has not been shown. Waiting for perfect proof is not an option either. The answer has to come from the numbers.
rest:
Step 1 of 6 · The finding

The decline is real, but it has a precise shape, and that shape already rules out some explanations

Before looking for causes, we need to know what they have to explain. The largest analysis brings together 137 studies, 965,264 young people aged 9 to 17 and 19 high-income or upper-middle-income countries, between 1981 and 2014. Estimated endurance (VO2max, the maximum oxygen the body uses per minute and per kilo) loses 3.3 mL/kg/min, or 7.3%, a decline the authors judge moderate. It affects 17 countries out of 19, boys more than girls.1 The decisive point is the pace: -2.2 mL/kg/min per decade in the 1980s, -1.6 in the 1990s, then -0.4 and -0.2 in the 2000s and 2010s, described as negligible.1

The loss of endurance almost stopped after 2000

137 studies, 965,264 young people aged 9 to 17, 1981 to 2014. Effect descriptors given by the authors; confidence interval for the last decade: -0.4 to 0.0. The “11 times” ratio is a calculation of this article. Source: Tomkinson et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2019.1

What this means

The loss is concentrated before 2000. A cause that dates only from the 2010s cannot explain most of this decline, even though it may add to it or prevent a recovery. This is the timing criterion.

France follows this pattern: among 15,420 young people aged 9 to 16 tested from 1999 to 2022, performance lost 2.31 standard deviations per decade before a break in 2010, and 0.15 after. A standard deviation is the usual spread of results: more than two in ten years is a clear shift, 0.15 is almost a halt.2

Second feature: selectivity. Among 2,216,320 young people aged 9 to 17 in 19 countries, hand grip strength rose by 19.4% between 1967 and 2017, or 3.8% per decade, faster after 2000.4 The standing broad jump (leg power) improves by 1.73 cm per decade across 10,940,801 young people, which the authors judge negligible, with a decline since 2000 in most countries.5 A review of 22 studies (96,522 young people, 17 countries) describes endurance rising until around 1986, falling again until around 2010-2012 and seeming to have reached a floor.3

Third feature: no clear drop in reported activity. The authors of the large analysis cite reviews according to which activity and sport participation have not changed in recent decades, while judging the trends unclear.1 In France, the share of 6-17 year olds reaching the recommendation did not change significantly between 2006 and 2015.6

What this means

The decline is fast and then almost stopped, it affects endurance more than strength, and it is not accompanied by a clear collapse in reported activity. Any credible cause has to fit this: we apply this filter, first to the most cited one.

Step 2 of 6 · Screens

Screens go with a little less movement, but the link is small and the timing fits poorly

What is claimed: more screen time goes with a little less activity and a little more fat. The link is small, measured mostly on television, and nothing read shows that it explains the decline in endurance.

The size of the link. A 2004 meta-analysis of young people aged 3 to 18 finds, for television time and physical activity (141,505 young people), r = -0.096; for video games and computer use (119,942 young people), -0.104; for television and fat mass (44,707 young people), 0.066.8 A coefficient r runs from -1 to +1, and its square gives the share of variation that two measures have in common: about 0.9%, 1.1% and 0.4% (calculation of this article).

Screen time shares only about 1% of its variation with physical activity

Squares of the correlations (0.096, 0.104, 0.066), calculation of this article. Corrected for measurement error, the television-activity correlation is -0.129 (about 1.7%). Source: Marshall et al., International Journal of Obesity, 2004.8

What this means

Knowing how many hours a young person spends in front of the television explains only about 1% of the difference between their activity and that of another. The authors judge the link with fat mass too small to have clinical significance.8 This work predates smartphones.

More recent syntheses point the same way. A review of 232 studies and 983,840 young people links more than 2 hours of television a day to lower fitness and a less favourable body composition.9 A 2019 review of reviews (13 reviews, only one of good quality) finds, for cardiorespiratory fitness, two reviews that speak of strong evidence and two of weak evidence, and settles on “weak and inconsistent”; its authors note that screen time was mostly self-reported and that data on mobile devices were very limited.10 The WHO judges its recommendation to limit sedentary time strong but of low certainty, without being able to set a threshold.14

The direction. According to a commentary on the 2019 review, it contains no follow-up and no trial: we cannot say whether television makes children fat or whether overweight children watch more television.11 A review of 29 reviews finds weak links with self-reported screen time, close to zero with sedentary time measured by sensor, and does not conclude that there is a cause.13 The only experimental evidence read: randomised trials aiming to reduce sedentary time lower BMI by 0.81 on average (interval from -1.44 to -0.17).9 That is a result on weight, not on endurance.

What remains is a picture that looks like proof: with age, activity falls and screens rise.

With age, activity falls and screens rise, but not exactly together

Activity: Esteban 2014-2016. Screens: ESEN 2017 survey, share under 2 h a day (34.6, 17.0 and 8.4%); the share above 2 h is its complement to 100 (calculation of this article). Two different surveys. Source: French “Report Card” 2022.7

What this means

From 6-10 to 11-14 years, activity falls and screens rise: this is the picture cited against screens. But at 15-17 years, boys' activity rises again (from 34 to 40%) while screens keep rising, and age changes everything at once: puberty, homework, lower secondary school, autonomy. The graph shows coexistence, not a cause.

The timing. This is where the accusation weakens. Between 2006 and 2015, daily screen time among French young people rose by about 25 minutes for 6-10 year olds, by 1 h 15 for 11-14 year olds and by almost 2 hours for 15-17 year olds.6 Over the same period, the share of young people reaching the recommendation did not change significantly,6 and the loss of endurance had already almost stopped (step 1). If screens were the main driver of the decline, the fastest decline should coincide with the steepest rise in screen time. It is the opposite.

The scope is limited: the series are of different kinds, I have not read a screen series for the 1980s and 1990s, when the loss was greatest, and screens may have prevented a recovery. The timing does not point to them as the main cause, that is all.

Verdict of the step (reading of this article)
  • Link: solid but small (r of about -0.1, or about 1% of shared variation).
  • Direction: not established. No trial read on endurance; the trials on sedentary time concern weight.
  • Timing: fits poorly with the moment of the decline in endurance.
  • Lever: weight goes down in trials of reducing sedentary time; the effect on endurance was not read.

Screens are not cleared, but they are not the demonstrated cause. One factor is often invoked alongside them: sleep, which screens are supposed to shorten.

Step 3 of 6 · Sleep

Sleep is shortening slowly and is weakly linked to movement, with the direction unknown

What is claimed: young people probably sleep a little less than at the start of the twentieth century and better sleep goes with better fitness, but neither the direction nor the timing is established.

The trend. A 2012 review of data published from 1897 to 2009 finds that children's actual sleep decreases by 0.73 minute per year, or about 7 minutes per decade (calculation of this article). These durations are mostly self-reported, a method that overestimates actual sleep according to the authors.16 In France, 43.0% of lower secondary students and 42.2% of upper secondary students report difficulty falling asleep more than once a week, more among girls (about 50%) than boys (about 35%).19 This is a frequency figure, with no duration and no trend.

The link. A 2021 review includes six articles, 5,797 young people aged 6 to 19, 11 countries: more sleep and better sleep go with better physical fitness, though the summary does not specify how solid the whole is.17 The link between screens and sleep is judged weak by the 2019 review.10

The direction. A study of 470 Spanish 8-year-olds, with sleep and activity sensors, tests both directions. More light activity goes with shorter night sleep (B = -0.18) but more efficient sleep (B = 0.19); in the other direction, more sleep predicts less light activity (B = -0.10) and no effect on vigorous activity.18 The B values are in the units of each measure: we read their sign and their smallness. The relationship runs both ways and does not take the form “more sleep, therefore more movement” (reading of this article, as the page read had no author conclusions).

The timing. Seven minutes less per decade over more than a century is a slow, steady phenomenon. The decline in endurance was fast and then stopped. A slow cause explains poorly a decline that changed pace.

What this means

Sleep is probably linked to movement, but the direction is open, the effects read are small and the timing does not fit. Sleeping matters, but sleep is not shown to be a driver of the decline in endurance. Girls report the most difficulty falling asleep and are the least likely to reach 60 minutes: a coincidence at this stage, not a mechanism.

Verdict of the step (reading of this article)
  • Link: weak (six studies, one measured sample of 470 children).
  • Direction: not established, probably both ways.
  • Timing: fits poorly (slow decline).
  • Lever: no trial read showing that lengthening sleep raises endurance.

We have tested private behaviours. Now we turn to the institution that reaches every child and whose hours are written down: school.

Step 4 of 6 · School sport

School sport is a demonstrated lever, not a demonstrated cause of the decline

What is claimed: PE hours are short, school activity programmes improve endurance on average, but nothing read shows that cut hours explain the decline. Two questions need separating: is school a cause of the decline, and is it a lever to correct it?

The hours. The European Commission (Eurydice) compiled in 2013 the recommended annual hours of physical education: from 37 hours in Ireland to 108 in France in primary school, and 108 in France in secondary school, the highest level. Between 2006-2007 and 2011-2012, they did not change in most countries, France included.22 The French timetable has about 3 hours of PE a week in primary and lower secondary school, 2 hours in upper secondary.7 Worldwide, UNESCO gives in 2013 about 97 minutes a week in primary and 99 in secondary (116 and 143 in 2000),20 and finds in 2021-2022 that only 42.7% of primary schools, 16.3% of lower secondary schools and 9.1% of upper secondary schools reach the set minimum (120 minutes in primary, 180 in secondary).21

What these hours can contribute. PE time is not effort time. In a meta-analysis on secondary school (25 studies, 15 of them pooled), the share of lessons spent in moderate to vigorous activity is 40.5% (34.8 to 46.2%), or 48.6% in lower secondary and 35.9% in upper secondary, below the 50% target.23 Applying these shares to French timetables gives the budget of one week.

Even if fully delivered, PE lessons cover only a small part of the weekly target

Timetables: French report 2022. Effort shares per lesson: 2017 meta-analysis (5 studies in lower secondary, 10 in upper secondary). The 87 and 43 minutes (21% and 10% of 420) are a calculation of this article, which assumes that all lessons take place and last the full hour.7,14,23

What this means

At best, lower secondary PE provides about a fifth of the WHO target, upper secondary PE a tenth: it cannot do the job alone. A pilot project in Rennes (126 upper secondary students, one school) nevertheless finds that 85% reach 60 minutes on a day with PE against 23% on a day without, which cannot be generalised.7

The lever. Can school at least improve endurance? Yes, on average and modestly. A meta-analysis of 40 studies (39 randomised trials, 17,880 children for endurance) finds a mean effect of 0.36 (0.25 to 0.46), judged small to moderate, of low certainty: in a future programme, the effect could range from -0.21 to 0.93, so sometimes be zero. Programmes of 24 weeks or more (0.45 against 0.28) and of 3 or more sessions a week (0.44 against 0.26) do better, as a lead.25 Another meta-analysis (43 studies, 27,626 young people) finds 0.28.26 A review of PE itself (24 studies) counts 16 positive results, 14 neutral and 3 negative, and concludes that the most intense lessons contribute consistently.24

The cause? Official hours did not fall in France between 2006 and 2012, whereas the country lost most of its endurance before 2010. I have read no French series of the hours actually delivered before 2006. So official hours do not point to school as a cause, but they measure neither cancelled lessons nor intensity.7

Verdict of the step (reading of this article)
  • Link: not read directly for hours; school activity trials show a gain in endurance.
  • Direction: established as a lever (randomised trials), not as a cause of the decline.
  • Timing: official hours stable in France since 2006; no older series read.
  • Lever: yes, modest (0.28 to 0.36), low certainty, better if the programme is intense and regular.

School occupies part of the week. What remains is the rest: how children get there and the environment they live in.

Step 5 of 6 · Journeys, neighbourhood, safety

Journeys, neighbourhood and safety: plausible leads, with almost no numbers on their effect

What is claimed: journeys could bring movement and bring it only in part, and parents cite safety as the first obstacle. For urban planning and safety, I have read no study with numbers linking them to young people's endurance or to its decline: an unknown of this research, not a negative result.

What is measured. According to the 2022 French report, which draws on several surveys, 40.2% of children aged 6 to 10 go to school by an active mode (35% of boys, 45% of girls). Across all home-school journeys, 40.0% are made on foot (37.6%) or by bike (2.4%) and 60.0% by motorised mode, including 31.7% by car; 35.7% are under 1 km and 50.4% under 2 km.7

Half of home-school journeys are under 2 km, but only 4 in 10 are made on foot or by bike

Distances: 2019 mobility survey; modes: year not specified in the extract read. “Other motorised modes” (60.0 minus 31.7) is a calculation of this article. Distances and modes concern the same journeys and do not add up. Source: French “Report Card” 2022.7

What this means

The potential exists: if half of journeys are under 2 km, some of those made by car could be made on foot or by bike. As an example calculation, two 15-minute walks make 30 minutes a day, or half of the recommended 60 minutes. But these figures describe a snapshot: I have read no series showing that this share has fallen since the 1980s, nor any study showing that young people who walk to school have better endurance.

Safety, as parents put it. In the same report, 97% of parents say they choose their child's mode of transport according to its safety. 55% cite lack of safety as the first obstacle to active modes, and 44% distance.7 This is a perception: it explains choices, but it measures neither the real danger nor the effect of those choices on fitness.

Urban planning and environment. For parks, cycle paths and density, the extracts read contain only recommendations, with no numbers.7 The only thing found is a strong association between endurance and income inequality across 18 countries between 2000 and 2014: countries moving closer to equality have a better trend. This is a correlation between countries, with no mechanism.1 ANSES also notes more sedentary behaviour among young people from less advantaged backgrounds.15

Verdict of the step (reading of this article)
  • Link: not read for journeys and urban planning.
  • Direction: not established.
  • Timing: not read (no long series on the share of active journeys).
  • Lever: not read for endurance. Active journeys count towards the 60 minutes according to ANSES.15

It remains to set the whole against the objections, and to look at the factor these causes are supposed to influence: weight.

Step 6 of 6 · The objections

What can bring the reasoning down, and what is still unknown

A demonstration that does not answer its objections is worth little. Here are six, from the most serious to the least serious.

The direction may be the reverse

A young person who is out of shape gets breathless, avoids effort and retreats to the screen: the supposed cause would be a consequence. The 2019 commentary says so for television, and the study of 470 children shows effects in both directions for sleep.11,18 I have read no follow-up over time that would rule out this possibility for endurance.

A third factor may drive everything

Social background may act on screens, sleep, journeys and activity all at once (step 5): the raw figures for each cause are to be read as upper bounds.1,15

Weight is the best-quantified factor, and it is contested

The authors of the international analysis write that the increase in fat mass explains 35 to 70% of the decline in endurance, based on earlier work: it is the largest share attributed to a single factor in the texts read. But in the same analysis, the share of overweight young people is associated, before 2000, with better endurance trends (contrary to expectation, they say), and negligible afterwards.1 In Quebec, the comparison of 3,725 students aged 6 to 17 with those of 1982 gives a VO2max gap of -17.7% in boys and -12.2% in girls at age 17, which the authors say is not attenuated by standardising for body mass.28 Weight is also downstream of diet, movement and sleep: probably a path through which the other causes act, not a competing cause.

Measures are imperfect and the evidence predates phones

Screen time and activity are mostly self-reported, endurance is estimated by equation. Screen studies weigh heavily on television, with little data on mobile devices, and low to medium quality: in the 2024 review (102 meta-analyses), 95 present a medium to high risk of bias.10,12 Endurance series stop in 2014 or 2022: a zone of ignorance, not proof of innocence.

Nobody has divided the decline among the causes

The authors of the international analysis speak of a network of factors.1 No study read says what share of the decline belongs to each cause: any ranking would be invented.

The answer to the problem

The question was which causes are backed by numbers, with what level of evidence, and which we can act on without waiting. Here is the answer, at the level of certainty the readings allow.

Cause by cause: what is established, what is weak, what has not been read

Qualitative synthesis of steps 2 to 5. No cell contains a new number. “Not read” means that no source opened for this article allows an answer, not that the answer is no.

Solid

The decline in endurance is real, especially before 2000, and affects endurance more than strength. The link between screen time and activity exists but is small (about 1% of common variation).

Probable but not demonstrated

Acting through school improves endurance on average, modestly (randomised trials, low certainty). A significant share of the decline also runs through fat mass (35 to 70% according to cited work), but the comparison between countries does not simply find it before 2000, and income inequalities are associated with the trend.

Weak

Screens as the main driver (timing, evidence predating phones), sleep as a cause (weak link, open direction, decline too slow) and the fall in PE hours as a cause in France (official hours stable since 2006).

Unknown

The role of journeys, urban planning and safety (no study with numbers read), the share of each cause, the effect of recent digital uses, and whether limiting screens or lengthening sleep raises endurance.

In one sentence: no single cause is demonstrated, and the one that dominates the debate is among the least supported. We can, however, act without waiting on what has trials behind it, movement at school, in intensity and in regularity, and on what costs little. A cause of the decline and a lever to correct it are not the same thing.

What to put in place

From the best documented to the least documented. The testing frequency is an editorial choice, based on the length of the programmes read, not on study data.

  1. Measure the starting point with the fitness test on this page.It places the child or adolescent against age and sex reference points: an estimate, not a diagnosis. Redo it every 3 to 6 months, under the same conditions: a small change can come from the error of the test.
  2. Aim for 60 minutes a day on average over the week.This is the WHO recommendation for 5-17 year olds (moderate evidence, strong recommendation).14 Since PE provides at best a fifth (lower secondary) or a tenth (upper secondary), most of it has to come from elsewhere: clubs, outdoor play, journeys.7
  3. Prefer regularity and intensity to volume.Three sessions a week that make you breathless, for at least 24 weeks: these are the programmes with the best effects, as a lead of low certainty.24,25
  4. Try active journeys when school is close.Start with one day a week, after checking the safety of the route, the first obstacle cited by parents. No data read measures the gain in endurance: the page's test will tell you whether it works for you.7
  5. Replace rather than ban when it comes to screens.The ANSES benchmark of 2 hours of leisure screen time a day is a threshold of caution, and the WHO sets no precise limit.14,15 ANSES advises replacing screen time with activity, even short sessions. Do not expect this measure alone to raise endurance.
  6. Protect sleep for its own sake, and look closely at adolescent girls.Nothing read shows that sleeping more raises endurance, but more than 4 in 10 lower and upper secondary students have difficulty falling asleep.19 At 15-17, 16% of girls reach 60 minutes against 40% of boys: ANSES recommends targeting adolescent girls and modest backgrounds.7,15

Abnormal breathlessness, chest pain or feeling unwell during effort justify medical advice before making a child run more.

What these figures do not say
  • These are group averages, mostly from high-income countries, and associations. No study read divides the decline among the causes.
  • Journeys, urban planning and safety have no study with numbers read here; the budget in step 4 is an order of magnitude.

Frequently asked questions

Should I remove screens so my child moves more?

The numbers do not justify it as a single measure: the link is small and nothing read shows that removing screens raises endurance. Replacing part of screen time with activity is, however, recommended by ANSES.8,15

Does sleeping more improve endurance?

We do not know. The studies read show weak links, running in both directions, with no trial.17,18

Would more PE hours be enough?

They would help, but not alone: even if fully delivered, current hours cover at best a fifth of the weekly target in lower secondary school. School programmes improve endurance modestly.7,25
